locator: §2.4 Generation of the set of result rows, paragraph on the result expression list
claim: For a simple SELECT, SQLite calculates each result row by evaluating the result expressions with respect to one input row, or one row group for an aggregate query.
quote: Each result row is calculated by evaluating the expressions in the result expression list with respect to a single row of input data or, for aggregate queries, with respect to a group of rows.

locator: SELECT List, paragraph on output column names
claim: PostgreSQL names an output column by writing AS output_name after the expression that computes it.
quote: To specify the name to use for an output column, write AS output_name after the column's expression.

claim: SQLite writes a string constant in single quotes and encodes an embedded single quote as two single quotes in a row, not with backslash escapes.
quote: A string constant is formed by enclosing the string in single quotes ('). A single quote within the string can be encoded by putting two single quotes in a row - as in Pascal. C-style escapes using the backslash character are not supported because they are not standard SQL.

claim: PostgreSQL writes a string constant in single quotes and escapes an embedded single quote by doubling it; a double quote is not the string delimiter.
quote: A string constant in SQL is an arbitrary sequence of characters bounded by single quotes ('), for example 'This is a string'. To include a single-quote character within a string constant, write two adjacent single quotes, e.g., 'Dianne''s horse'. Note that this is not the same as a double-quote character (").

claim: By default a PostgreSQL SELECT returns all candidate rows including duplicates, and SELECT DISTINCT removes duplicate rows.
quote: SELECT DISTINCT eliminates duplicate rows from the result. SELECT DISTINCT ON eliminates rows that match on all the specified expressions. SELECT ALL (the default) will return all candidate rows, including duplicates. (See DISTINCT Clause below.)

claim: When neither ALL nor DISTINCT is written, SQLite behaves as if ALL were specified and returns the entire set of result rows.
quote: If the simple SELECT is a SELECT ALL, then the entire set of result rows are returned by the SELECT. If neither ALL or DISTINCT are present, then the behavior is as if ALL were specified.

claim: For SELECT DISTINCT, SQLite removes duplicate rows from the computed result set, comparing the values of each result row with IS DISTINCT FROM so that two NULLs are considered equal.
quote: If the simple SELECT is a SELECT DISTINCT, then duplicate rows are removed from the set of result rows before it is returned. For the purposes of detecting duplicate rows, values are compared using the IS DISTINCT FROM operator. Thus two NULL values are considered to be equal.

title: PostgreSQL 18 Documentation, 7.3: Select Lists
why: States that DISTINCT compares all column values of result rows and treats nulls as equal for duplicate elimination.

claim: PostgreSQL treats two result rows as distinct if they differ in at least one column value, and considers null values equal in that duplicate comparison.
quote: Obviously, two rows are considered distinct if they differ in at least one column value. Null values are considered equal in this comparison.

locator: §2 Simple Select Processing, four-step outline, steps 1–2
claim: SQLite's illustrative steps determine the input data from the FROM clause, or one empty row when FROM is absent, and then filter that input with the WHERE expression.
quote:
1.  FROM clause processing: The input data for the simple SELECT is determined. The input data is either implicitly a single row with 0 columns (if there is no FROM clause) or is determined by the FROM clause.

2.  WHERE clause processing: The input data is filtered using the WHERE clause expression.

claim: SQLite says its step-by-step description is purely illustrative and no SQL engine is required to follow that or any other specific process.
quote: It is important to keep in mind that this is purely illustrative - in practice neither SQLite nor any other SQL engine is required to follow this or any other specific process.

claim: PostgreSQL does not define the order in which subexpressions are evaluated, so operator and function inputs are not necessarily evaluated left-to-right.
quote: The order of evaluation of subexpressions is not defined. In particular, the inputs of an operator or function are not necessarily evaluated left-to-right or in any other fixed order.

locator: §2 Operators, and Parse-Affecting Attributes, paragraph after the operator list
claim: SQLite performs integer arithmetic when both operands are integers and no overflow would result, switches to floating-point arithmetic when either operand is real or integer arithmetic would overflow, and truncates integer division toward zero.
quote: The other arithmetic operators perform integer arithmetic if both operands are integers and no overflow would result, or floating point arithmetic, per IEEE Standard 754, if either operand is a real value or integer arithmetic would produce an overflow. Integer divide yields an integer result, truncated toward zero.

claim: PostgreSQL's division row truncates integral results toward zero, with 5 / 2 → 2 and (-5) / 2 → -2, while 5.0 / 2 → 2.5000000000000000 for the numeric operand.
quote:
| Division (for integral types, division truncates the result towards zero)                         |
|                                                                                                   |
| 5.0 / 2 → 2.5000000000000000                                                                      |
|                                                                                                   |
| 5 / 2 → 2                                                                                         |
|                                                                                                   |
| (-5) / 2 → -2                                                                                     |
